newsitem.title: GERMANY: German union group opposes EMU-based welfare cuts.
newsitem.headline: German union group opposes EMU-based welfare cuts.

text.p: The German Trade Union Federation (DGB) said on Tuesday that it would only back European monetary union if no further welfare cuts and reductions in state spending were required for it.
The DGB issued a statement during its jobs summit in Berlin calling on the German government to commit itself to no further such savings measures in the run-up to a single currency.
The statement added that for the DGB to back EMU, the government had to recognise there was room to interpret the Maastricht Treaty flexibly.
"Landing exactly on three percent is not a condition for entry into monetary union," it said.

The statement also called on the government to promote European-wide infrastructure investment programmes that would create jobs across the continent and in which what it called public companies would take part.
In Germany, it listed those companies as the Post AG post office, the Bahn AG railways and the now privatised Deutsche Telekom.
Earlier, DGB chief Dieter Schulte said the government must promise to back the inclusion of specific employment policies in the up-coming negotiations on the Maastricht Treaty.
The DGB was also demanding the Social Chapter on working conditions should form part of the treaty on monetary union.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Monday tried to play down talk that Bonn was taking a softer stance on the deficit criteria needed to join monetary union.
He said Germany still intended to cut its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product as the Maastricht Treaty aims for, and not ask for a looser interpretion of the rules.
"Three percent is three percent and it will stay that way," Waigel said.
